813.title: Zaynab bint Khuzaymah
813.hook: almost all that is left of her is a name the poor gave her, and she died soon after the marriage
813.howItsDone: Muslims remember Zaynab bint Khuzaymah among the mothers of the believers by her title umm al-masakin, and feeding the poor is a regular act of charity on this path, often given in someone's memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the other Zaynab, and the wives measuring their hands. Your line was: the longest hands. What did your hands make or do for someone? Day eight hundred thirteen.

Some people leave diaries. Some leave buildings. Some leave a single name, and the name says a great deal. Of today's mother of the believers, the sources keep very little: no long speeches, no famous scenes. The early biographers say she married the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and died not long after. And they say what people called her: umm al-masakin. The mother of the poor. Today: Zaynab bint Khuzaymah.
screen: `SOME LEAVE ONLY A NAME.` → `THE SOURCES KEEP LITTLE.` → `UMM AL-MASAKIN.`

segments.voice: It's worth being honest at the start. The hadith collections this path usually draws on say little about Zaynab bint Khuzaymah. What we have comes mostly from the biographers, Ibn Sa'd among them, and it is short: her marriage, her early death, and her name. But consider what a title like that suggests. Nobody is called the mother of the poor for one good afternoon. Some readers hear in it the people at her door, the ones who kept coming back because someone kept feeding them: a reputation built meal by meal. And the name sits right inside what the Qur'an praises. In surah seventy-six, the righteous are described as feeding the needy, the orphan and the captive, for love of Allah, and saying, in effect: we feed you for Allah's sake alone; we want no reward from you and no thanks. Food with no invoice attached. In Bukhari, the Prophet says that the one who looks after the widow and the poor is like one who strives in the way of Allah, or like one who prays all night and fasts all day. So the mother of the poor was doing the kind of work the Prophet set alongside prayer and fasting. There's a quiet lesson in how little we know. Zaynab's life comes down to us almost entirely as what she did for people who couldn't repay her. If only one line of your story survived, it could do worse than that. Mother of the poor.
screen: `THE SOURCES SAY LITTLE.` · `A NAME EARNED MEAL BY MEAL.` · `WE FEED YOU FOR ALLAH ALONE.` · `LIKE ONE WHO PRAYS ALL NIGHT.` · then, large: `MOTHER OF THE POOR.`

segments.voice: The practice: feed the poor in her memory. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the last meal you ate. Taste it again for a moment. Now think of someone near you, in your town or on your street, who may not have had one today. You don't need to solve hunger in two minutes. Just choose one meal you could give this week: to a food bank, a neighbor, someone outside a shop. Picture handing it over, with no thanks expected. If you pray, you can remember Zaynab by name. The bell holds the time.
Zaynab bint Khuzaymah. A mother of the believers who died soon after her marriage, and whose story survives mostly as a name: the mother of the poor. Today's word.
Your line: mother of the poor. Today, give one meal, or the price of one, to someone who can't repay you, and don't wait for thanks. Day eight hundred thirteen.

814.title: Juwayriyyah's freed people
814.hook: a captive comes to ask for help with her freedom, and her marriage sets her people free (Abu Dawud)
814.howItsDone: Muslims honor Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith among the mothers of the believers, retelling from Sunan Abi Dawud how her marriage led to the freeing of her people, and many learn the words of remembrance taught to her in Sahih Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, whose story survives as a name. Your line was: mother of the poor. Did a meal go to someone who couldn't repay you? Day eight hundred fourteen.

A battle is over, and the losing tribe's people are captives. Among them is the daughter of their chief. She has made an agreement to buy her own freedom, and she can't pay it. So she does something brave: she goes straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to ask for help. Aisha, watching her come to the door, tells us in Abu Dawud's collection what happened next. Today: Juwayriyyah's freed people.
screen: `A CHIEF'S DAUGHTER, CAPTIVE.` → `SHE CAN'T PAY FOR HER FREEDOM.` → `SHE GOES TO ASK.`

segments.voice: The tribe was the Banu al-Mustaliq, and the woman was Juwayriyyah, daughter of their chief, al-Harith. In the report, she tells the Prophet plainly who she is, what has happened to her, and that she needs help paying for her freedom. He offers her something better: he will pay what she owes and marry her. She accepts. Then comes the part the story is really about. The news goes around the camp: the Prophet has married Juwayriyyah. And the companions, who were holding her people as captives, said, in effect: these are now the Prophet's in-laws. How can we keep his relatives as captives? And they let them go. The report counts it: through that marriage, a hundred households of the Banu al-Mustaliq were set free. Then Aisha adds a sentence of her own. She says she knew of no woman who was a greater blessing to her people than Juwayriyyah. One woman walked in to ask about her own freedom. Her people walked out free. Look at the chain. Her courage to ask. His answer, larger than the question. And then the companions, who weren't commanded to do anything, choosing on their own to free people because of a new family tie. Honor for one person spread outward until it became freedom for many. One more glimpse: Sahih Muslim has Juwayriyyah sitting in her place of prayer from dawn until the late morning, remembering Allah. The woman who brought freedom to a whole tribe is remembered at prayer, too. A blessing to her people.
screen: `SHE TELLS HIM WHO SHE IS.` · `HE PAYS AND MARRIES HER.` · `HOW CAN WE HOLD HIS IN-LAWS?` · `A HUNDRED HOUSEHOLDS FREED.` · then, large: `A BLESSING TO HER PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: free someone from a burden. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone near you carrying something they can't put down on their own. A chore that's swallowing them, an apology they're waiting for, a grudge you're holding against them, a worry nobody has helped with. Which of those could you lift? Not everything. One thing. See yourself lifting it: doing the task, saying the word, letting the grudge go, sitting with the worry. If you pray, you can ask to be a blessing to the people around you. The bell holds the time.
Juwayriyyah's freed people. The chief's daughter who asked for help with her freedom, and whose marriage to the Prophet led the companions to free her people. Today's word.
Your line: a blessing to her people. Today, lift one burden off one person, and let it spread. Day eight hundred fourteen.

815.title: Umm Habibah
815.hook: Abu Sufyan's daughter, who believed while her father opposed the Prophet, and emigrated to Abyssinia
815.howItsDone: Muslims honor Umm Habibah, Ramlah bint Abi Sufyan, among the mothers of the believers and among the emigrants to Abyssinia; her rule of mourning from Sahih al-Bukhari is part of how Muslims learn the limits of mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Juwayriyyah, who walked in to ask and whose people walked out free. Your line was: a blessing to her people. Whose burden did you lift? Day eight hundred fifteen.

Her father would come to lead the Quraysh against the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. That father was Abu Sufyan, and his daughter Ramlah, known as Umm Habibah, had become a Muslim anyway. She left Mecca with the emigrants across the sea to Abyssinia, far from her family. Years of opposition between her house and her faith. And then one day, in Ibn Ishaq's telling, her father walks into her room in Medina. Today: Umm Habibah.
screen: `HER FATHER LEADS THE OPPOSITION.` → `SHE BELIEVES ANYWAY.` → `HER FATHER WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: Start in Abyssinia. Umm Habibah went there as an emigrant with her first husband, and her first marriage ended there, far from home. Sunan Abi Dawud preserves what happened next: the marriage between her and the Prophet was arranged in Abyssinia, with the Negus, the Christian king who had sheltered the Muslims, giving the dowry on the Prophet's behalf. The daughter of a leader of the opposition, married to him in a Christian king's land. Now the visit. Ibn Ishaq says Abu Sufyan came to Medina, still not a Muslim, trying to shore up a treaty his side had broken. He went to his daughter's room and was about to sit on the Prophet's bedding. She folded it away. He asked whether she thought the bedding too good for him, or him too good for it. She answered that it was the Messenger's place, and he was still a man who worshipped idols. Strong words to a father. The sirah keeps them as a picture of faith set above a family's pride. But hold a second report beside it, this one in Bukhari. Years later, when news reached her of Abu Sufyan's death, Umm Habibah, on the third day, called for perfume and put it on. She said she had no need of perfume, but she had heard the Prophet say a believing woman should not mourn more than three days, except for a husband. She did mourn her father. She just kept her mourning within what she had been taught. Faith before family pride did not mean faith without family love. It meant knowing which came first. Faith before family pride.
screen: `A MARRIAGE MADE IN ABYSSINIA.` · `SHE FOLDS AWAY THE BEDDING.` · `IT IS THE MESSENGER'S PLACE.` · `SHE MOURNS HER FATHER THREE DAYS.` · then, large: `FAITH BEFORE FAMILY PRIDE.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep faith when family disagrees. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place, if there is one, where what you hold most deeply and what your family expects don't line up. It might be about faith, or about something else you care about. Breathe in, and name what you won't let go of. Breathe out, and name one thing you love about that family member anyway. Hold both. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Umm Habibah. Abu Sufyan's daughter, who believed while her father opposed the Prophet, married the Prophet in Abyssinia, and still mourned her father when he died. Today's word.
Your line: faith before family pride. Today, hold to one thing that matters to you, and say one kind thing to the relative who sees it differently. Day eight hundred fifteen.

816.title: Safiyyah and Maymunah
816.hook: Safiyyah, taunted for her Jewish family, is defended by the Prophet ﷺ, and Maymunah's house becomes a place where a boy learns the night prayer
816.howItsDone: Muslims honor Safiyyah bint Huyayy and Maymunah bint al-Harith among the mothers of the believers; the Prophet's answer to the taunt is retold from Jami' al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Abbas's night in Maymunah's house from Sahih al-Bukhari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umm Habibah, the folded bedding and the three days of mourning. Your line was: faith before family pride. Did you find a kind word for someone who sees it differently? Day eight hundred sixteen.

A woman is crying, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, walks in and asks why. Safiyyah tells him what she heard. Someone in the household, Hafsah, had called her the daughter of a Jew. It was meant to sting, and it did. Safiyyah came from a noble family of a Jewish tribe of Arabia, and that remark turned her family into an insult. What he says next is preserved in Tirmidhi's collection. Today: Safiyyah and Maymunah.
screen: `A WOMAN IN TEARS.` → `THE DAUGHTER OF A JEW?` → `WHAT HE SAYS NEXT.`

segments.voice: He doesn't tell Safiyyah to forget her family, or to be ashamed of it. He turns the taunt inside out. You are the daughter of a prophet, he tells her, meaning Aaron. Your uncle is a prophet, meaning Moses. And you are married to a prophet. So what is there for her to boast over you? Then he says: Hafsah, be mindful of Allah. Look at what he did. The very thing used against Safiyyah, her descent, became the thing he honored. The Qur'an names Aaron and Moses among the prophets, and Muslims honor them as such. He pointed her to that line and said: this is yours. A taunt about where she came from was answered by honoring where she came from. He defended her. Now Maymunah, the other name in today's title. Tradition remembers her as the last woman he married. One scene with her in it is gentle and ordinary. Her nephew, Abdullah ibn Abbas, still a boy, slept over at her house one night, and he tells us in Bukhari what he saw: the Prophet rising in the night, making his ablution, and standing to pray. The boy got up and stood beside him to join in. And the Prophet took hold of him and moved him around to his right side, where he should stand. Ibn Abbas grew up to be a teacher himself, and this lesson he learned in Maymunah's house. One wife, defended against a taunt. One wife whose home was open for a boy to learn. He defended her.
screen: `DAUGHTER OF A PROPHET, AARON.` · `YOUR UNCLE IS MOSES.` · `THE TAUNT TURNED INTO HONOR.` · `A BOY LEARNS IN MAYMUNAH'S HOUSE.` · then, large: `HE DEFENDED HER.`

segments.voice: The practice: defend someone from a taunt. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a remark you've heard aimed at someone's family, their background, their accent, their faith. Maybe in a group chat, maybe at work. Now find what the Prophet found: something true and good in the very thing they were mocked for. Hold that sentence until it's ready to say. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to say it. The bell holds the time.
Safiyyah and Maymunah. Safiyyah, taunted for her Jewish family and told she was the daughter of a prophet; Maymunah, in whose house a boy learned the night prayer. Today's word.
Your line: he defended her. Today, when someone is mocked for where they come from, say one true, good thing about it. Day eight hundred sixteen.

817.title: Maria and the eclipse
817.hook: Maria bears him a son, Ibrahim, who dies as a baby, and on the day of an eclipse he says the sun and moon don't eclipse for anyone's death (Bukhari)
817.carry: the eyes weep, the heart grieves
817.howItsDone: When a solar or lunar eclipse happens, Muslims gather for salat al-kusuf, the eclipse prayer, with long recitation and bowing; at a death, Muslims often say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to God and to Him we return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Safiyyah and Maymunah, and a taunt that didn't go unanswered. Your line was he defended her. Was there a moment you spoke up for someone, or wished you had? Day eight hundred seventeen.

The sky over Medina goes dim in broad daylight. The sun is being eaten from one side. On the ground, the town is already in mourning, because that same day a baby has died: Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. People look up, then look at each other, and the talk begins. Of course the sun went dark. The heavens are grieving his son. It's a kind thing to say. It would comfort a father. Today: Maria, her son, and what he said under that dark sky.
screen: `THE SUN GOES DIM BY DAY.` → `A BABY HAS DIED THE SAME DAY.` → `THE HEAVENS ARE GRIEVING?`

segments.voice: Ibrahim's mother was Maria, remembered as Maria the Copt. Tradition, in Ibn Sa'd's biographies, says she came to Medina from Egypt, sent by its ruler. Some count her among the mothers of the believers; others give her a different standing, as the mother of his son. She's honored either way, and this is where our part on the mothers ends. Now the boy. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Anas tells of the day they went in to Ibrahim as he was dying. The Prophet's eyes filled with tears. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, surprised, asked: you too, messenger of God? And he answered: this is mercy. Then he said the line we carry today: the eyes weep, the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And he spoke to the child: we are saddened by your parting, Ibrahim. Notice what that sentence allows. Tears, openly. Sorrow, named. And one limit: no words of protest against God. Then the eclipse. Another report in Bukhari, from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, says the sun was eclipsed on the day Ibrahim died, and people said it was for his death. The Prophet answered them: the sun and the moon are two of the signs of God, and they are not eclipsed for anyone's death or life. When you see it, pray and call on God until it clears. He could have let the kind story stand. It was flattering, and it was about his own child. He corrected it on the day of his grief. That's why Muslims keep an eclipse prayer, salat al-kusuf: the dark sky becomes a time to pray, not a message about any one person. Grief that is real, and truth that isn't bent to comfort it.
screen: `MARIA, MOTHER OF IBRAHIM.` · `THIS IS MERCY.` · `NOT FOR ANYONE'S DEATH OR LIFE.` · `THE ECLIPSE BECOMES A TIME TO PRAY.` · then, large: `THE EYES WEEP, THE HEART GRIEVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grieve honestly, without a story on top. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let one loss come to mind, large or small, recent or old. Don't explain it. Don't look for a sign in it. If tears come, let them; in the report, they were called mercy. Just say to yourself what is true: this hurt, and I miss them. If you pray, you can say the line from the Qur'an that Muslims say at a loss: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." If not, just stay with the plain sorrow, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Maria and the eclipse. Maria the Copt, mother of Ibrahim, and the day the sun went dark and the Prophet said it was not for his son. Today's word.
Your line: the eyes weep, the heart grieves. Today, when something sad comes up, name it plainly to one person, without dressing it up or explaining it away. Day eight hundred seventeen.

818.title: Fatimah al-Zahra
818.hook: his youngest daughter, of whom he said, Fatimah is a part of me (Bukhari)
818.howItsDone: Muslims speak of Fatimah with deep honor, often adding a blessing after her name; Shi'a Muslims in particular remember her in prayers and gatherings, and Muslim families name daughters after her.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maria and the eclipse, and a father who wept and still told the truth about the sky. Your line was the eyes weep, the heart grieves. Did you name something sad plainly? Day eight hundred eighteen.

A young woman crosses a room in Medina, and another woman watching her notices something. She walks exactly like her father. Same pace, same way of carrying herself. The watcher is Aisha, and she tells this herself in Sahih al-Bukhari. The father is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and he is ill. The daughter is Fatimah. He calls out to her, welcome, my daughter, and sits her beside him. Then he leans close and whispers something, and she starts to cry. He whispers again, and she laughs. Aisha asks what he said. Fatimah won't tell her. Today: Fatimah, and the title she carries.
screen: `SHE WALKS EXACTLY LIKE HER FATHER.` → `A WHISPER: SHE WEEPS.` → `ANOTHER: SHE LAUGHS.`

segments.voice: Fatimah kept the secret while her father lived. After he died, Aisha asked again, and this time she told, and the reports in Bukhari give her answer. The first whisper: he would not recover from this illness. So she wept. The second, in one telling: she would be the first of his family to follow him; in another, she would be a leader among the women of paradise. So she laughed. Look at what that means. The news that comforted her was that she would not be apart from him for long. That closeness runs through every report about them. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, Aisha says that when Fatimah came in, he would stand up for her, kiss her, and seat her in his own place; and when he came to her, she did the same for him. A father standing up for his daughter. And in Bukhari he says it outright: Fatimah is a part of me, and whoever angers her angers me. Now the title. Muslims call her Fatimah al-Zahra. In Arabic, al-Zahra means the radiant one, the shining one. The reports we just heard don't use it; it's a name later generations gave her, and they explain it in different ways. Sunni and Shi'a Muslims both use it and both honor her deeply. In Shi'a devotion her name is spoken in prayers and gatherings, and given to daughters. Across all of them, one picture holds: a daughter who walked like her father, sat in his seat, and was called a part of him.
screen: `FIRST WHISPER: HE WOULD NOT RECOVER.` · `SECOND: SHE WOULD FOLLOW HIM SOON.` · `HE STOOD UP FOR HER.` · `AL-ZAHRA: THE RADIANT ONE.` · then, large: `FATIMAH IS A PART OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a daughter. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a daughter: yours, a niece, a student, a friend's girl, or yourself as someone's daughter. See her coming into the room. In your mind, stand up for her, the way he stood for Fatimah, and give her your seat. What would you want her to hear from you? Hold one sentence of honor for her, plain and true. If you pray, you can make a quiet du'a for her. If not, just keep her in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Al-Zahra. The radiant one: the title Muslims give Fatimah, the Prophet's daughter, whom he called a part of him. Today's word.
Your line: a part of him. Today, tell a daughter in your life, or a parent if you're the daughter, one specific thing you honor in her. Day eight hundred eighteen.

819.title: Fatimah's hands
819.hook: her hands are rough from the mill, and she's given the tasbih instead of a servant (Bukhari)
819.howItsDone: Muslims say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar before sleep, following this hadith, and the set is often called the tasbih of Fatimah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Zahra, the radiant one: a daughter who walked like her father and sat in his seat. Your line was a part of him. Who did you tell what you honor in them? Day eight hundred nineteen.

Two flat stones, one on top of the other, with a wooden handle set in the top one. You pour grain in the hole and turn, and turn, and turn, and flour creeps out the edge. That's a hand mill, and in Medina someone had to turn one every day, or there was no bread. In the house of Ali and Fatimah, that someone was Fatimah. The Prophet's daughter, the one he called a part of him, had hands that showed it. Today: Fatimah's hands, and what her father gave her for them.
screen: `TWO STONES AND A HANDLE.` → `NO TURNING, NO BREAD.` → `THE PROPHET'S DAUGHTER AT THE MILL.`

segments.voice: Ali describes her work in a report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. She turned the mill until it marked her hand. She carried water in a skin until the strap marked her. She swept the house until her clothes were dusty, and kept the fire under the pot. When captives came to Medina, Ali suggested she go to her father and ask for a servant. Bukhari tells what came next. She went, he wasn't home, and she left word. That night he came to their house, sat down between them, and taught them words for bedtime: Allahu akbar thirty-four times, subhanallah thirty-three, alhamdulillah thirty-three. And he said this is better for you than a servant. We met that set of words on an earlier day. Today, look at the hands instead. He didn't tell her the work was beneath her. He didn't take it away, either. Aisha, asked what the Prophet did at home, says in Bukhari that he served his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. Work first, in the house, with his own hands; then prayer. So what did Fatimah receive? Not a way out of the mill. A way to carry it. The words come at the end of the day, after the work is done, when the hands are finally still. Ali said in a report in Bukhari that he never left them off after that night. Some readers see here a household that lived on little, where the tiredness itself was met with remembrance. The hands stayed rough. The night got words.
screen: `THE MILL MARKED HER HAND.` · `ASK FOR A SERVANT.` · `WORDS AT BEDTIME INSTEAD.` · `WORK FIRST, THEN PRAYER.` · then, large: `BETTER FOR YOU THAN A SERVANT.`

segments.voice: This week ran from Zaynab, mother of the poor, through Juwayriyyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Maria, to Fatimah, the Prophet's daughter. Now the practice: your own hard work, then remembrance. Sit, and think back over the day your hands have had. What did they do today? Dishes, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a child's coat. Let each task come up and go. Then rest them. If you pray, you can say subhanallah, alhamdulillah, Allahu akbar, slowly, as many times as the sit allows. If not, just feel the tired hands go still. The bell holds the time.
Fatimah's hands. Rough from the mill, and given words for the end of the day instead of a servant. Today's word.
Your line: better than a servant. Today, do one chore you'd rather hand off, all the way through with your own hands, and when it's done, stop for a short remembrance. Day eight hundred nineteen.
